questiontext.text: A topological ordering of a directed graph is a linear order of its vertices such that:

answer.text: For every edge u→v, u appears before v

feedback.text: Correct — every directed edge points forward in the ordering.

answer.text: For every edge u→v, v appears before u

feedback.text: That reverses the requirement; edges must point forward.

answer.text: Vertices are sorted by ascending degree

feedback.text: Topological order is about edge direction, not degree.

answer.text: Vertices are sorted by their labels

feedback.text: Labels are irrelevant; edge constraints define the order.

generalfeedback.text: A topological sort lays out the vertices so that all dependencies (edges) point from earlier to later.

questiontext.text: A topological ordering exists if and only if the graph is:

feedback.text: Correct — a cycle would force a vertex to precede itself, so acyclicity is required.
Connectivity is neither necessary nor sufficient; acyclicity is the condition.
Topological order is defined for directed graphs.
A complete directed graph has cycles and no topological order.

generalfeedback.text: Exactly the DAGs admit a topological ordering; any directed cycle makes it impossible.

questiontext.text: Kahn's algorithm for topological sort repeatedly does what?

answer.text: Removes a vertex with in-degree 0 and decrements its neighbors' in-degrees

feedback.text: Correct — in-degree-0 vertices have no unmet dependencies and go next.

answer.text: Removes the vertex with the largest out-degree first

feedback.text: Out-degree does not drive Kahn's algorithm.

answer.text: Relaxes edges using a priority queue by weight

feedback.text: That describes Dijkstra, not topological sort.
That is the MST red-blue framework, unrelated here.

generalfeedback.text: Kahn's algorithm maintains a queue of in-degree-0 vertices, emitting them and reducing neighbors' in-degrees until all are placed.

questiontext.text: What is the time complexity of topological sort (Kahn's or DFS-based)?

feedback.text: Correct — each vertex and edge is processed a constant number of times.
That is Bellman-Ford, not topological sort.
That is Floyd-Warshall.
Topological sort is linear in the graph size.

generalfeedback.text: Both Kahn's algorithm and DFS post-order run in O(V + E).

questiontext.text: A directed graph that contains a cycle has no valid topological ordering.

feedback.text: Correct — a cycle makes a consistent linear order impossible.
Cyclic directed graphs cannot be topologically sorted.

questiontext.text: A topological ordering can be produced by reversing the DFS post-order of a DAG.

feedback.text: Correct — reversing DFS finishing times yields a valid topological order.
Reversed DFS post-order is a standard way to topologically sort a DAG.

questiontext.text: A topological ordering exists exactly when the graph is a ______ (three-letter English acronym for a directed acyclic graph).

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about topological sort are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It applies only to directed acyclic graphs

feedback.text: Yes — a cycle would make the ordering impossible.

answer.text: Kahn's algorithm processes in-degree-0 vertices using a queue

feedback.text: Yes — that is the core of Kahn's method.

answer.text: It requires edge weights to be non-negative

feedback.text: No — topological sort ignores weights entirely.
No — it runs in O(V + E).

generalfeedback.text: Topological sort: defined on DAGs, computed by Kahn's queue of in-degree-0 vertices or reversed DFS post-order, in O(V + E) time; weights are irrelevant.
